Marketing Campaigns — Exploratory Data Analysis & Hypothesis Testing¶

Course: Applied Data Science with Python
Objective: Explore customer characteristics, product spending, sales channels and campaign responses; test the four hypotheses in the project brief.

Run the notebook from top to bottom. It reads marketing_data.csv from the same folder. The data dictionary supplied with the project describes the variables.

2. Cleaning and feature engineering¶

  • Parse Dt_Customer as a date.
  • Standardize uncommon marital-status labels (Alone, YOLO, Absurd) to Other for grouped analysis.
  • Impute missing income using the median within Education × Marital_Status groups; fall back to Education median, then overall median.
  • Derive age using the maximum birth year in the dataset as a transparent reference year, total children, total product spending and total purchases across web/catalog/store channels.

Note: The dataset does not provide a fixed analysis date, so age is calculated relative to the maximum observed birth year (1996) for internal comparisons. If your instructor specifies another reference year, change REFERENCE_YEAR below.

In [20]:
# Step 1: Clean column names
df.columns = df.columns.str.strip()

# Step 2: Convert Income to numeric
df["Income"] = pd.to_numeric(
    df["Income"]
    .astype(str)
    .str.replace(r"[$,\s]", "", regex=True),
    errors="coerce"
)

# Step 3: Clean marital status categories
df["Marital_Status"] = df["Marital_Status"].replace({
    "Alone": "Other",
    "YOLO": "Other",
    "Absurd": "Other"
})

# Step 4: Impute missing income using group median
group_median = df.groupby(
    ["Education", "Marital_Status"]
)["Income"].transform("median")

df["Income"] = df["Income"].fillna(group_median)

# Step 5: Fill remaining missing values using education median
education_median = df.groupby("Education")["Income"].transform("median")
df["Income"] = df["Income"].fillna(education_median)

# Step 6: Fill any remaining missing values with overall median
df["Income"] = df["Income"].fillna(df["Income"].median())

# Step 7: Verify the result
print("Income data type:", df["Income"].dtype)
print("Missing income values:", df["Income"].isna().sum())
print(df["Income"].head())

df["Dt_Customer"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Dt_Customer"], errors="coerce", dayfirst=True)

df["Marital_Status"] = df["Marital_Status"].replace({

})

income_col = "Income"
group_median = df.groupby(["Education", "Marital_Status"], dropna=False)[income_col].transform("median")
df[income_col] = df[income_col].fillna(group_median)
education_median = df.groupby("Education")[income_col].transform("median")
df[income_col] = df[income_col].fillna(education_median)
df[income_col] = df[income_col].fillna(df[income_col].median())

REFERENCE_YEAR = int(df["Year_Birth"].max())  # dataset-relative reference, not current age
df["Age"] = REFERENCE_YEAR - df["Year_Birth"]
df["TotalChildren"] = df["Kidhome"] + df["Teenhome"]

purchase_cols = ["NumWebPurchases", "NumCatalogPurchases", "NumStorePurchases"]
df["TotalSpending"] = df[spend_cols].sum(axis=1)
df["TotalPurchases"] = df[purchase_cols].sum(axis=1)

print("Missing income after imputation:", df[income_col].isna().sum())
print("Reference year used for age:", REFERENCE_YEAR)

4. Outlier review and treatment¶

Outliers are flagged using the 1.5×IQR rule. Rather than deleting customer records, the notebook creates a winsorized copy for selected skewed continuous variables. Original variables remain available for business interpretation. The threshold summary is printed below.

In [28]:
outlier_cols = ["Income", "Age", "TotalSpending"]
outlier_summary = []
df_winsor = df.copy()
for col in outlier_cols:
    q1, q3 = df[col].quantile([0.25, 0.75])
    iqr = q3 - q1
    low, high = q1 - 1.5 * iqr, q3 + 1.5 * iqr
    count = ((df[col] < low) | (df[col] > high)).sum()
    outlier_summary.append({"variable": col, "lower_bound": low, "upper_bound": high, "outlier_count": int(count)})
    df_winsor[col] = df[col].clip(lower=low, upper=high)
display(pd.DataFrame(outlier_summary))

7. Hypothesis testing¶

All tests use a 5% significance level (alpha = 0.05). The tests below operationalize the brief's hypotheses with the available fields. Results indicate association, not necessarily causation.

  1. Older customers prefer in-store purchases: Pearson correlation between Age and NumStorePurchases.
  2. Customers with children prefer online shopping: compare web purchases for customers with children vs. no children using Welch's t-test.
  3. Store sales may be cannibalized by other channels: correlation between store purchases and combined web + catalog purchases. A negative correlation is consistent with the idea but does not prove cannibalization.
  4. US outperforms the rest of the world in purchase volume: compare total purchases for US vs. non-US customers using Welch's t-test. Country codes are used as provided; US is the United States.
In [37]:
alpha = 0.05
results = []

# H1: Age vs in-store purchases
r1, p1 = stats.pearsonr(df["Age"], df["NumStorePurchases"])
results.append({"Hypothesis": "Older age associated with more store purchases",
                "Test": "Pearson correlation", "Statistic": r1, "p_value": p1,
                "Decision": "Reject H0" if p1 < alpha else "Fail to reject H0"})

# H2: children vs web purchases
with_children = df.loc[df["TotalChildren"] > 0, "NumWebPurchases"]
without_children = df.loc[df["TotalChildren"] == 0, "NumWebPurchases"]
t2, p2 = stats.ttest_ind(with_children, without_children, equal_var=False, nan_policy="omit")
results.append({"Hypothesis": "Customers with children make more web purchases",
                "Test": "Welch independent t-test", "Statistic": t2, "p_value": p2,
                "Decision": "Reject H0" if p2 < alpha else "Fail to reject H0"})

# H3: store purchases vs other-channel purchases
other_channel = df["NumWebPurchases"] + df["NumCatalogPurchases"]
r3, p3 = stats.pearsonr(df["NumStorePurchases"], other_channel)
results.append({"Hypothesis": "Store purchases negatively associated with web+catalog purchases",
                "Test": "Pearson correlation", "Statistic": r3, "p_value": p3,
                "Decision": "Reject H0" if p3 < alpha else "Fail to reject H0"})

# H4: US vs all other countries
us_purchases = df.loc[df["Country"].eq("US"), "TotalPurchases"]
nonus_purchases = df.loc[~df["Country"].eq("US"), "TotalPurchases"]
t4, p4 = stats.ttest_ind(us_purchases, nonus_purchases, equal_var=False, nan_policy="omit")
results.append({"Hypothesis": "US customers have higher total purchases than non-US customers",
                "Test": "Welch independent t-test", "Statistic": t4, "p_value": p4,
                "Decision": "Reject H0" if p4 < alpha else "Fail to reject H0"})

display(pd.DataFrame(results))
print("Group means:")
print("Web purchases, with children:", round(with_children.mean(), 2),
      "| without children:", round(without_children.mean(), 2))
print("Total purchases, US:", round(us_purchases.mean(), 2),
      "| non-US:", round(nonus_purchases.mean(), 2))
print("Store vs other channel correlation:", round(r3, 3))

9. Conclusion and limitations¶

Use the printed tables, p-values and charts above to write conclusions based on the observed data. A p-value below 0.05 is evidence against the corresponding null hypothesis, but effect sizes and group means should also be considered. The dataset is observational; correlations do not establish causality. Country sample sizes differ substantially, and the country with the highest count of acceptances is not necessarily the country with the highest acceptance rate. The age reference year is dataset-relative because a fixed analysis date was not specified in the brief.
